text: You already built one chart with one values file. Now we give it separate values for dev, staging, and production — and this lesson is going to feel familiar, because it's deliberately the same pattern you used with Terraform's variable files back in the IaC course. If that course's lesson on workspaces and tfvars files stuck with you, most of what follows here is just that idea, applied to Kubernetes manifests instead of cloud resources.

Start with a base values.yaml holding sane defaults — one replica, the current image tag, modest resource requests, ingress turned off. Think of this as effectively your dev configuration: the values you'd get if nobody overrode anything at all, and the file every other environment's overrides are measured against.

A second file, values-prod.yaml, holds only what's different for production — not a full copy of every key, just six replicas instead of one, bigger resource requests and limits, and ingress turned on with a real hostname. You layer it on top of the base file with two stacked --values flags, and Helm merges them left to right, so the later file's keys win on anything it specifies, while everything it leaves out quietly falls back to values.yaml.

Here's the direct parallel. terraform apply with a var-file supplied environment-specific values to one resource definition — helm upgrade with stacked --values flags does the exact same job for one chart. Where the pattern breaks is state: Terraform workspaces isolate state files, but a Helm release's state lives inside the cluster itself, tracked by release name and namespace. So instead of selecting a workspace, you pair a distinct release name — like myapp-prod — with a distinct namespace, and that's what keeps your environments from colliding.

That's the whole pattern: one chart, layered values files, and release name plus namespace standing in for what a workspace did on the Terraform side. Next lesson, we put a release through its full lifecycle — upgrading it, rolling it back, and reading its release history.
